title: Agent Orchestration Pattern Decision Guide
summary: Choose direct tools, deterministic workflows, manager-agent delegation, handoffs, parallel work, or human routing from control and evidence needs.
prerequisites: A decomposed workflow with known decisions, tools, risks, and ownership

sections.title: Choose the least complex sufficient pattern
paragraphs: Start with the smallest pattern that satisfies the control, evidence, and risk requirements. Use one agent with direct tools when one instruction set and one accountable owner can complete the work. Use a deterministic sequential workflow when order, validation, or compliance must be guaranteed. Use independent parallel branches only for independent, read-only or isolated work, and define an explicit join and conflict policy before starting.

Use manager+tools when specialist agents should provide bounded results while a manager retains control, combines outputs, and owns the final response. Use a handoff when a specialist should become the active owner and speak directly to the user. Use human routing when authorization, ambiguity, consequence, or accountability cannot safely be delegated.

More agents add handoff, context, latency, cost, and failure surfaces. They are not a default quality feature. A parallel branch must not mutate the same external state without an explicit isolation and reconciliation design. A join must reject unresolved conflicts. A vote count is not evidence that a result is true.

Use these questions in order: Who is accountable for the final output? Which state can change? Must steps occur in a fixed order? Are branches genuinely independent? Who may authorize the consequential action? What evidence must be retained for recovery and audit? If a simpler pattern answers these questions safely, prefer it.

code.label: Pattern selection questions
code.code:
1. Direct tools: one owner, one instruction set, limited branching.
2. Sequential: fixed order, validation gates, or compliance requirements.
3. Parallel: independent read-only or isolated branches, explicit join, conflict rejection.
4. Manager+tools: bounded specialists, manager keeps control and final output ownership.
5. Handoff: a specialist becomes the active owner and communicates with the user.
6. Human route: authorization, ambiguity, consequence, or accountability requires a person.

sections.callout: Always name exactly one accountable final-output owner and the human authority who can stop, approve, reconcile, or roll back the workflow.

sections.title: Record the orchestration decision
paragraphs: Define ownership of state, approvals, user communication, final output, and recovery. Decide what context crosses each boundary, how sensitive data is filtered, how duplicate actions are prevented, and how partial branches are reconciled.

The required determinism level is a reasoned requirement, not a universal numerical score. LOW means variation is acceptable within stated safety limits. MEDIUM means important steps or validations must be controlled. HIGH means order, approval, or compliance must be guaranteed.

A complete record should make a later review possible without reconstructing intent from chat logs. It should state why simpler patterns failed, what the timeout and cancellation behavior is, and what evidence will establish whether the policy worked.

code.label: Filled decision record: case 1
code.code:
Workflow outcome: Produce a validated monthly inventory report from three read-only warehouse exports and publish it only after schema and reconciliation checks.
Steps and dependencies: ingest exports -> validate each schema -> normalize item identifiers -> reconcile totals -> generate report -> publish approved artifact.
Required determinism: HIGH WITH REASON: validation, reconciliation, and publication order must be guaranteed; publication must not occur after a failed check.
Risk/approval points: publication of the report -> operations lead; any mismatch above the stated tolerance -> operations lead.
Chosen pattern: SEQUENTIAL
Why simpler patterns fail: direct tools allow an optional validation step to be skipped; manager+tools does not by itself guarantee order or a fail-closed publication gate.
Control owner: inventory workflow controller.
Final-output owner: operations lead, accountable for the published report.
State owner and consistency model: workflow controller, durable state with one status transition per step and an idempotency key per reporting period.
Context passed: reporting period, export references, schema version, normalized totals, validation results, reconciliation result, approval status.
Context withheld/redacted: worker credentials, unrelated customer data, raw secrets, full export rows after normalization unless needed for audit.
Join/handoff contract: each step receives a versioned input and returns status, evidence reference, and output reference; DONE means validation passed and the output is durably stored.
Timeout/cancellation: cancel before publication when the controller receives a cancellation; mark the run CANCELLED, stop downstream steps, and retain completed evidence; timeout moves the run to REVIEW rather than publishing.
Duplicate/retry control: idempotency key is reporting-period plus export-version; retries may repeat read-only work but publication checks the key and reconciles the existing artifact first.
Partial-failure policy: FAIL CLOSED for validation, reconciliation, or publication; retain partial artifacts for diagnosis and do not publish.
Observability: trace each step and transition; metrics for duration, retries, and failed checks; audit record for approval, cancellation, and publication.
Rollback: revoke the unpublished artifact; for a published correction, return to the prior approved report and require a new approval.
Evaluation cases: normal complete exports, ambiguous item identifier, failed schema, timeout before publication, cancellation during normalization, duplicate retry, conflicting totals, adversarial extra column.

sections.callout: A decision record is an operational contract. It is not a claim that a particular model, vendor, or API guarantees execution of the contract.

sections.title: Expected evidence and verification
paragraphs: The expected evidence is a decision record plus evaluation traces showing that the selected pattern assigns one accountable owner, preserves required context, enforces approval, and handles timeout, duplicate, and partial-failure cases.

Compare the chosen pattern with a simpler baseline on task success, unsupported actions, handoff accuracy, latency, cost, and recovery. Use a fixed test set and state the assumptions behind every cost and latency value. If a value has not been measured, record UNKNOWN rather than presenting an estimate as fact.

Inject a failed specialist and a conflicting parallel result. Confirm that the owner can cancel, reconcile, or roll back without repeating external effects. Joins must reject unresolved conflicts, and agreement by multiple branches must not substitute for source validation.

Retain evidence for stop and recovery, idempotency and reconciliation, and observability. Label deterministic synthetic traces as synthetic. These traces demonstrate the application's routing, approval, timeout, and recovery policy, not model or vendor capability.
Revisit the choice when tasks, tools, risks, deployment constraints, or model behavior change. The same pattern is not automatically suitable for every provider or deployment.

sections.callout: The trace examples are policy fixtures. They do not report an actual run and do not establish any model or vendor feature.

sections.title: Worked case: deterministic sequential reporting
paragraphs: Situation: an operations team must turn three read-only warehouse exports into one monthly inventory report. The report must not be published if a schema check or reconciliation check fails. The exports are independent inputs, but the steps after ingestion depend on validated results.

Decision: choose SEQUENTIAL. A parallel ingestion stage is compatible with this choice only if each branch is isolated and the join rejects missing or conflicting results. The accountable final-output owner is the operations lead. The workflow controller owns execution state, but it does not become the business approver.

Comparison assumptions for this synthetic planning exercise: direct tools are assumed to require 1 agent run, 4 tool calls, 1.0 relative latency unit, and 1.0 relative cost unit. Sequential is assumed to require 5 controlled steps, 3.0 relative latency units, and 2.0 relative cost units. These are planning assumptions, not measurements. Actual latency and cost are UNKNOWN until instrumented in the target deployment.

The sequential option is accepted because its extra assumed latency and cost buy an explicit order and fail-closed gates. Direct tools lose because a prompt-level instruction is not sufficient evidence that validation always precedes publication. Manager+tools loses because the manager can combine outputs but does not inherently provide a guaranteed state machine. Parallel-only loses because independent ingestion does not remove the required ordered validation and publication gates.

Dependencies are export availability, schema version, identifier normalization, reconciliation, and approval. Risks include malformed input, conflicting totals, duplicate publication, timeout, cancellation, and uncertain publication state. Recovery is a review state, reconciliation by idempotency key, and rollback to the prior approved report.

Sequential            Controller; operations lead    Fixed step order and approval          Explicit fail-closed transitions         2.0 / 3.0 relative       WINS: order and evidence are required

sections.callout: The comparison is populated with explicit assumptions for learning. Replace every relative value with measured deployment data before using it for procurement or capacity planning.

sections.title: Worked case: human routing for a consequential refund
paragraphs: Situation: a support assistant receives a request to refund a disputed high-value order. The order record contains an address mismatch and the customer has not clearly authorized the requested destination. A refund can create an external financial consequence.

Decision: choose HUMAN ROUTE. The assistant may gather facts and prepare a proposed action, but a designated support supervisor must resolve the ambiguity and authorize the refund. The supervisor is the accountable final-output owner for the customer-facing decision. A system owner remains accountable for safe routing, audit, and prevention of duplicate actions.

Comparison assumptions for this synthetic planning exercise: direct tools are assumed to have 1.0 relative latency unit and 1.0 relative cost unit; manager+tools is assumed to have 1.5 relative latency units and 1.5 relative cost units; human route is assumed to have 4.0 relative latency units and 4.0 relative cost units because it includes a review queue. These are not measurements. Actual latency, staffing cost, and refund-processing behavior are UNKNOWN until measured in the target deployment.

Human route wins because authorization, ambiguity, consequence, and accountability are present. Direct tools lose because an agent must not silently decide the disputed authorization. Manager+tools loses because adding a manager does not transfer legal or organizational accountability to a qualified human. Handoff loses because a specialist speaking directly to the customer could still act without the required approval. Parallel branches lose because agreement between branches does not establish authorization or truth.

The assistant passes only the minimum necessary context: order identifier, disputed amount, relevant policy references, mismatch facts, customer request, and proposed next actions. It withholds unrelated personal data and credentials. The approval record includes the supervisor identity, decision, timestamp, policy basis, and idempotency key. If the external payment state is uncertain, the system reconciles by that key before any retry.

sections.callout: Human routing is not a failure of automation. It is the selected control when the organization requires a human authority for authorization, ambiguity, consequence, or accountability.

sections.title: Worked case: independent parallel branches with a rejecting join
paragraphs: Situation: a team needs three independent, read-only summaries of separate documents. Each branch receives a document identifier and extraction instructions. No branch writes shared state. A joiner checks that every required branch completed, validates citations, and rejects contradictory claims for human review.

Decision: choose PARALLEL for the isolated extraction stage, followed by a controlled join. The final-output owner is the research lead. The joiner owns the technical decision to accept or reject the set, but it does not own the final published interpretation.

This choice would be wrong if branches edited the same record, depended on one another's intermediate results, or were being used merely to count agreement. A failed branch produces an incomplete set and blocks the join. A conflict produces REVIEW, not a majority decision.

Synthetic planning assumptions: three branches in parallel have an assumed 1.2 relative latency units and 1.8 relative cost units, while a sequential baseline has 3.0 relative latency units and 1.8 relative cost units. These values are illustrative assumptions, not execution results. Actual values are UNKNOWN until measured.

code.code:
Option              Ownership                  Dependencies                         Risks and controls                         Assumed cost/latency       Why it loses or wins
Direct tools         Research lead              One agent reads all documents           Context overload; missed document       1.0 / 2.5 relative       Loses: separate evidence streams needed
Sequential            Research lead              Document 1 before 2 before 3           Unnecessary waiting                       1.8 / 3.0 relative       Loses: no dependency between documents
Parallel              Research lead; joiner      Isolated reads and explicit join       Failure or conflict blocks publication  1.8 / 1.2 relative       WINS: work is independent and read-only
Manager+tools         Manager; research lead     Specialist summaries and synthesis      Synthesis may hide disagreement           2.0 / 1.8 relative       Loses: join contract is clearer here

Human route           Research lead              Human reads each document               Higher assumed delay and effort            3.0 / 4.0 relative       Loses for routine extraction; handles REVIEW

sections.callout: Parallelism is justified by independence, not by a desire for more agents. The join must define completeness, conflict handling, and the single final-output owner.

sections.title: Learner variation: change the inputs
paragraphs: Start from the inventory-report case. Change the inputs as follows: the three sources are now live systems that can be updated, the report must trigger a replenishment order, the order requires a supervisor's approval, and one source may be unavailable for up to ten minutes. The business also requires that a retry never create a second order.

Choose one of DIRECT TOOLS, SEQUENTIAL, PARALLEL, MANAGER+TOOLS, HANDOFF, or HUMAN ROUTE. Write a short decision record. Name the control owner and exactly one final-output owner. State what happens on timeout, cancellation, conflicting values, and an uncertain order side effect. Compare your choice with the simpler direct-tools baseline.

Do not select parallel merely because the sources are separate. Explain whether branches are isolated and how the replenishment order is prevented from being issued before the required join and approval.

sections.title: Answer key and feedback
paragraphs: A strong answer chooses SEQUENTIAL with a HUMAN ROUTE approval gate, or describes the combination precisely as a sequential workflow containing a human approval step. The primary pattern is not selected by a universal score. It follows from the changed control requirements: mutable systems, a consequential replenishment order, required approval, unavailable input, and duplicate prevention.

The control owner can be a workflow controller or operations system owner. The one accountable final-output owner should be the supervisor who approves the replenishment order and resulting report. The controller may execute transitions, but it must not silently become the business approver.

A strong record makes the order explicit: read and validate sources, wait or route for missing input, reconcile values, request approval, issue the order with an idempotency key, verify or reconcile the external state, then publish the report. On timeout, stop or move to REVIEW rather than ordering. On cancellation, stop downstream work and retain a checkpoint. On conflicting values, reject the join and route for review. On an uncertain order result, reconcile using the idempotency key before retrying.

Direct tools is a weak baseline because a single instruction does not establish durable gates, approval evidence, or safe recovery from an uncertain side effect. Parallel read-only acquisition may be a useful subpattern only when each branch is isolated and the join blocks downstream action until all required inputs are valid.

Feedback rubric: full credit requires one final-output owner, explicit human authority, high determinism with a reason, dependency order, fail-closed or review behavior for missing and conflicting data, idempotency or reconciliation for the order, and traces for timeout, cancellation, conflict, and uncertain side effects. Partial credit applies when the pattern is reasonable but one of these contracts is missing. Revise an answer that treats branch agreement as truth, treats estimated costs as measured facts, or claims a model or vendor guarantees the policy.

code.label: Reference answer record
code.code:
Workflow outcome: Produce a replenishment recommendation and issue at most one approved replenishment order.
Steps and dependencies: collect sources -> validate availability and schemas -> normalize identifiers -> reconcile values -> route missing or conflicting inputs to review -> request supervisor approval -> issue order with idempotency key -> reconcile external order state -> publish report.
Required determinism: HIGH WITH REASON: mutable external state, required approval, fixed gates, and no duplicate order.
Risk/approval points: replenishment order -> supervisor; unresolved conflict or missing source -> supervisor.
Chosen pattern: SEQUENTIAL with HUMAN ROUTE approval gate.
Why simpler patterns fail: direct tools do not provide durable approval and recovery gates; parallel-only work cannot safely control the shared mutable order; manager+tools does not replace the required human authority.
Control owner: replenishment workflow controller.
Final-output owner: supervisor approving the order and report.
State owner and consistency model: workflow controller with durable state transitions and one idempotency key per order intent.
Context passed: source references, normalized values, conflict details, proposed quantity, policy basis, approval status, idempotency key, external reconciliation result.
Context withheld/redacted: credentials, unrelated customer records, unnecessary raw source data.
Join/handoff contract: all required validated sources plus an explicit conflict status; approval requires supervisor identity and decision; DONE means external order state is reconciled and report is stored.
Timeout/cancellation: missing source timeout routes to REVIEW; cancellation stops before order if possible and records the checkpoint; an in-flight uncertain order requires reconciliation before any retry.
Duplicate/retry control: stable order-intent idempotency key and reconciliation lookup before retry.
Partial-failure policy: FAIL CLOSED before approval or order; RECONCILE after an uncertain external result; no report publication until required state is known.
Observability: trace transitions, approval, source status, join result, order request, reconciliation, cancellation, and publication; retain metrics and audit records.
Rollback: cancel an unissued order; if an order exists, follow the approved operational reversal process and publish a corrected report only after review.
Evaluation cases: normal sources, unavailable source, conflicting values, rejected approval, cancellation before order, timeout during order, duplicate retry, uncertain external result, adversarial extra field.

sections.callout: The answer key is a reasoning example. Equivalent records can be correct when they preserve the same ownership, authority, dependency, idempotency, recovery, and evidence contracts.

sections.title: Runnable offline exercise and fixtures
paragraphs: This self-contained exercise implements a bounded, provider-neutral orchestration policy. It uses only Python's standard library, performs no network access or external actions, and does not claim to have been executed here. Save the program as orchestration_exercise.py and run it with `python3 orchestration_exercise.py`. The program prints one deterministic decision line per fixture and then runs unittest assertions. Any mismatch causes a nonzero process exit.

The policy distinguishes top-level routing from a nested approval gate. HUMAN ROUTE means that human authorization, ambiguity, consequence, or accountability is the primary routing requirement. SEQUENTIAL + HUMAN ROUTE GATE means that the workflow controller retains fixed step order while a named human approval step blocks the consequential action. The changed replenishment case therefore uses sequential control with a human approval gate, rather than treating human review as an unrelated replacement for sequencing.

The original seven fixture names are retained. The shared-mutation fixture has been repaired to expect rejection, because a claim that work is both independent read-only and shared mutable is an invalid input, not a safe reason to select a different pattern. The other original expected decisions remain unchanged. Additional independent negative fixtures cover absent human authority, inconsistent claims, boolean, string, list, and null input shapes, unresolved conflict, and a missing accountable owner.

The supplied cost and latency values are explicitly assumed relative values. They are printed for comparison only, are not measurements, and do not rank models, providers, or vendors. Actual deployment cost and latency are UNKNOWN. Establish them by instrumenting the target deployment with a fixed evaluation set and a stated accounting method.

Independent changed-input task: starting from the inventory-report case, change the inputs to live mutable sources, a replenishment order, mandatory supervisor approval, a source that may be unavailable for ten minutes, and a no-duplicate retry requirement. The reference key in the fixture selects SEQUENTIAL + HUMAN ROUTE GATE. Its trace is: collect and validate sources -> normalize -> reconcile -> route missing or conflicting data to review -> request supervisor approval -> issue at most one order using an idempotency key -> reconcile the external order state -> publish the report. Timeout or cancellation stops before the order when possible. An uncertain order result requires reconciliation before retry. The single final-output owner is the supervisor; the workflow controller owns execution state and is not the business approver.

The policy follows the supplied decision-guide boundaries: exactly one accountable final-output owner, explicit human authority, rejection of unresolved conflicts, and an explicitly defined state owner and consistency model. It is an illustrative teaching policy, not a universal architecture recommender.

code.label: Standard-library offline exercise
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass
import io
import sys
import unittest


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Fixture:
    name: str
    data: object
    expected: str
    assumed_cost: float
    assumed_latency: float


BOOLEAN_FIELDS = (
    "mutable_state",
    "fixed_order",
    "independent_read_only",
    "approval_required",
    "ambiguity",
    "one_owner",
    "conflict",
    "human_authority",
    "approval_gate_in_sequential",
)


def reject(message):
    return "REJECT: " + message


def validate(data):
    if not isinstance(data, dict):
        return reject("input must be an object")
    missing = [field for field in BOOLEAN_FIELDS if field not in data]
    if missing:
        return reject("missing boolean field: " + missing[0])
    for field in BOOLEAN_FIELDS:
        if type(data[field]) is not bool:
            return reject("field " + field + " must be boolean")
    return None


def decide(data):
    """Return a bounded policy decision for one validated fixture."""
    shape_error = validate(data)
    if shape_error is not None:
        return shape_error

    if not data["one_owner"]:
        return reject("name exactly one final-output owner")
    if data["conflict"]:
        return reject("unresolved conflict requires review")
    if data["independent_read_only"] and data["mutable_state"]:
        return reject("parallel claim conflicts with mutable shared state")

    human_required = (
        data["approval_required"]
        or data["ambiguity"]
        or data["mutable_state"]
    )
    if human_required and not data["human_authority"]:
        return reject("human authority is required")

    if data["fixed_order"] and data["approval_gate_in_sequential"]:
        return "SEQUENTIAL + HUMAN ROUTE GATE"
    if data["approval_required"] or data["ambiguity"]:
        return "HUMAN ROUTE"
    if data["fixed_order"]:
        return "SEQUENTIAL"
    if data["independent_read_only"]:
        return "PARALLEL"
    return "DIRECT TOOLS"


def base(**overrides):
    value = {
        "mutable_state": False,
        "fixed_order": False,
        "independent_read_only": False,
        "approval_required": False,
        "ambiguity": False,
        "one_owner": True,
        "conflict": False,
        "human_authority": True,
        "approval_gate_in_sequential": False,
    }
    value.update(overrides)
    return value


# The first seven preserve the original fixture names and expected decisions.
# The shared-mutation expected value is deliberately repaired to fail closed.
fixtures = [
    Fixture("inventory gates", base(fixed_order=True), "SEQUENTIAL", 2.0, 3.0),
    Fixture("isolated document reads", base(independent_read_only=True), "PARALLEL", 1.8, 1.2),
    Fixture("single safe lookup", base(), "DIRECT TOOLS", 1.0, 1.0),
    Fixture("refund authorization", base(approval_required=True, ambiguity=True), "HUMAN ROUTE", 4.0, 4.0),
    Fixture(
        "negative shared mutation",
        base(mutable_state=True, independent_read_only=True),
        "REJECT: parallel claim conflicts with mutable shared state",
        1.0,
        1.0,
    ),
    Fixture(
        "negative unresolved conflict",
        base(independent_read_only=True, conflict=True),
        "REJECT: unresolved conflict requires review",
        1.8,
        1.2,
    ),
    Fixture(
        "negative missing owner",
        base(one_owner=False),
        "REJECT: name exactly one final-output owner",
        1.8,
        1.2,
    ),
]


# Independent changed-input task and reference key for the replenishment case.
learner_replenishment = Fixture(
    "changed learner replenishment",
    base(
        mutable_state=True,
        fixed_order=True,
        approval_required=True,
        human_authority=True,
        approval_gate_in_sequential=True,
    ),
    "SEQUENTIAL + HUMAN ROUTE GATE",
    3.5,
    4.5,
)
fixtures.append(learner_replenishment)


# Additional negative fixtures. Invalid shapes are intentionally separate cases.
fixtures.extend([
    Fixture(
        "negative absent human authority",
        base(approval_required=True, human_authority=False),
        "REJECT: human authority is required",
        4.0,
        4.0,
    ),
    Fixture(
        "negative inconsistent read-only mutable claims",
        base(independent_read_only=True, mutable_state=True, human_authority=True),
        "REJECT: parallel claim conflicts with mutable shared state",
        1.0,
        1.0,
    ),
    Fixture(
        "negative boolean shape",
        dict(base(), mutable_state=1),
        "REJECT: field mutable_state must be boolean",
        1.0,
        1.0,
    ),
    Fixture(
        "negative string shape",
        dict(base(), fixed_order="yes"),
        "REJECT: field fixed_order must be boolean",
        1.0,
        1.0,
    ),
    Fixture(
        "negative list shape",
        dict(base(), independent_read_only=[]),
        "REJECT: field independent_read_only must be boolean",
        1.0,
        1.0,
    ),
    Fixture(
        "negative null shape",
        dict(base(), approval_required=None),
        "REJECT: field approval_required must be boolean",
        1.0,
        1.0,
    ),
    Fixture(
        "negative unresolved conflict independent",
        base(conflict=True),
        "REJECT: unresolved conflict requires review",
        1.0,
        1.0,
    ),
    Fixture(
        "negative absent accountable owner independent",
        base(one_owner=False),
        "REJECT: name exactly one final-output owner",
        1.0,
        1.0,
    ),
])


class PolicyFixtureTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_every_fixture_matches_its_key(self):
        for fixture in fixtures:
            with self.subTest(fixture=fixture.name):
                self.assertEqual(decide(fixture.data), fixture.expected)



def main():
    for fixture in fixtures:
        actual = decide(fixture.data)
        status = "PASS" if actual == fixture.expected else "FAIL"
        print(
            f"{status} | {fixture.name} | decision={actual} | "
            f"assumed_cost={fixture.assumed_cost:.1f} | "
            f"assumed_latency={fixture.assumed_latency:.1f}"
        )

    stream = io.StringIO()
    result = unittest.TextTestRunner(stream=stream, verbosity=0).run(
        unittest.defaultTestLoader.loadTestsFromTestCase(PolicyFixtureTests)
    )
    print(
        f"SUMMARY | fixtures={len(fixtures)} | tests={result.testsRun} | "
        f"failures={len(result.failures)} | errors={len(result.errors)}"
    )
    if not result.wasSuccessful():
        print(stream.getvalue(), file=sys.stderr, end="")
        return 1
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

sections.callout: Expected output is a fixture expectation, not an execution report. The summary is computed by the program from the defined fixture list and unittest result. The exercise intentionally encodes a small fail-closed teaching policy. It does not establish model, vendor, runtime, latency, cost, authorization, cancellation, or external-system capabilities.

sections.title: Transfer the reasoning across deployments
paragraphs: The decision method is provider-neutral: define the application policy, ownership, state, approvals, boundaries, and evidence before selecting a deployment. The pattern names in this guide describe control arrangements, not guaranteed features of a model or vendor.

For Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Phi, NVIDIA, and Z.ai deployments, map the same contracts onto the specific runtime, gateway, tool layer, queue, identity system, storage, and human-review system used by that deployment. Verify the actual integration's cancellation, timeout, retry, idempotency, tracing, data handling, and approval behavior. Do not infer support for a pattern from a model name, provider name, or marketing description.

A deployment-specific record should identify the model and runtime versions, tool adapters, authentication boundary, state store, trace system, and measured evaluation results. If any capability or behavior has not been verified in that deployment, record UNKNOWN and define the test that would establish it.

The same application policy can therefore be transferred across these deployments without claiming that any one of them supports a particular orchestration feature. What changes is the implementation and the evidence, not the obligation to keep one final-output owner, clear human authority, explicit joins, and safe recovery.

code.label: Deployment transfer checklist
code.code:
Deployment: [model, runtime, gateway, version]
Control owner: [role/system]
Final-output owner: [exactly one role]
Human authority: [role and approval boundary]
State store and consistency model: [deployment-specific]
Tool and identity boundary: [deployment-specific]
Timeout and cancellation test: [result or UNKNOWN]
Idempotency and reconciliation test: [result or UNKNOWN]
Trace and audit retention: [deployment-specific]
Parallel isolation and join test: [result or UNKNOWN]
Unsupported-action test: [result or UNKNOWN]
Measured latency and cost: [values, assumptions, or UNKNOWN]
Evidence references: [trace, audit, evaluation case]

sections.callout: Provider-neutral means portable reasoning and explicit verification. It does not mean identical implementation, performance, or capability across deployments.

sections.title: Reusable blank decision record
paragraphs: Copy this blank record for a new workflow. Fill every field before approving an orchestration change. Use UNKNOWN for an unmeasured quantity and name the test or evidence that would establish it.

code.label: Blank reusable orchestration decision record
code.code:
Workflow outcome: [RESULT]
Steps and dependencies: [STEP -> PREDECESSOR]
Required determinism: [LOW | MEDIUM | HIGH WITH REASON]
Risk/approval points: [ACTION -> APPROVER]
Chosen pattern: [DIRECT TOOLS | SEQUENTIAL | PARALLEL | MANAGER+TOOLS | HANDOFF | HUMAN ROUTE]
Why simpler patterns fail: [EVIDENCE]
Control owner: [ROLE]
Final-output owner: [ROLE]
State owner and consistency model: [SYSTEM, RULE]
Context passed: [MINIMUM FIELDS]
Context withheld/redacted: [FIELDS]
Join/handoff contract: [INPUT, OUTPUT, DONE CONDITION]
Timeout/cancellation: [POLICY]
Duplicate/retry control: [IDEMPOTENCY OR RECONCILIATION]
Partial-failure policy: [FAIL CLOSED | COMPENSATE | DEGRADED]
Observability: [TRACE, METRICS, AUDIT]
Rollback: [RETURN TO PRIOR PATTERN/STATE]
Evaluation cases: [NORMAL, AMBIGUOUS, FAILURE, ADVERSARIAL]

sections.callout: Do not approve a record that leaves final ownership, human authority, conflict handling, duplicate prevention, or recovery undefined.
